   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`.    - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).

Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Low concern: As a single-wave cross-sectional household survey (Afrobarometer Round 7), longitudinal panel attrition does not apply. Item-level missingness across regression specifications is minimal (<1%, ranging from N = 44,887 in unadjusted individual-bribe-omitted models to N = 44,778 in full models and N = 44,546 for the Homesource models), although household survey non-response rates are not reported in the article.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern for causal inference / Some concern for descriptive association: Models adjust for individual utilities bribery, enumerator-assessed area piped water infrastructure, household lived poverty index, urban/rural status, respondent gender, regional non-utilities corruption, and country fixed effects, and authors explicitly disclaim causal claims. Nevertheless, the cross-sectional design leaves substantial potential for reverse causality/simultaneity (water scarcity inducing bribery) and unmeasured subnational confounding (regional economic output, local fiscal capacity, climate/aridity, and utility-specific institutional governance).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate (Some concern): The study does not measure formal de jure water law, regulatory institutions, or statutory rules; instead, it proxies de facto administrative corruption using household self-reports of paying bribes, gifts, or favors to government officials for utilities, averaged at the subnational region level. Construct specificity for water governance is weakened because the Afrobarometer question bundles water, sanitation, and electricity services together and codes respondents who never sought services identically to those who sought services without paying a bribe (zero).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Both exposure and outcomes are derived from same-source household survey self-reports (plus subjective enumerator observation of area piped infrastructure) without independent objective verification. The bribery measure conflates water, sanitation, and electric utilities, conflates non-applicants with bribe-free users, is vulnerable to social desirability/reporting bias, and fails to replicate in Afrobarometer Rounds 5 and 6 (showing a null association in Round 5 and a positive association in Round 6 and pooled Rounds 5-7, which the authors attribute to pre-CAPI interviewer walk-pattern bias).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Some concern (Weak-to-adequate): Water access is measured via a standardized 12-month recall survey question on how often the family went without enough clean water for home use, collapsed in primary models into a coarse binary indicator (anything other than 'always' coded as 1, meaning respondents lacking water 'many times' are coded as having access, though full 5-category ordered probit models and an Appendix sensitivity recoding are also reported) alongside self-reported source location (inside house, inside compound, outside compound). No objective physical water quality testing, meter continuity data, or technical JMP source verification is used.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Low-to-moderate concern (No information on pre-registration): No pre-analysis plan or protocol registration is reported. However, within-paper reporting transparency is strong: the authors report binary probit, full 5-category ordered probit, mixed-effects, PSU-level, leave-one-out regional corruption, and non-utilities corruption specifications, and candidly report null and opposite-signed estimates from Afrobarometer Rounds 5 and 6.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Some concern: The study uses Afrobarometer Round 7 (2016-2018) representative household surveys across 34 African countries employing Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) and GPS tracking to enforce random-walk respondent selection. However, the main text does not explicitly state individual respondent eligibility criteria, country selection criteria, survey response rates, or an explicit participant flow diagram, and coding non-seekers of utility services as zero in the bribery variable mixes service demand/contact into the exposure denominator.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors state that data come from Round 7 of the Afrobarometer representative household surveys conducted in 34 African countries between 2016 and 2018 (N = 44,778 in main full specifications), but they do not explicitly specify respondent eligibility criteria (e.g., age thresholds, household head/adult selection rules), why those 34 countries were included, or how missing observations were excluded between the total Round 7 sample and the analytical samples (N = 44,887, N = 44,778, and N = 44,546).
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 4 (Data and Methods), PDF Page 7 (p. 125); Table 1, PDF Page 7 (p. 125); Table 2, PDF Page 10 (p. 128); Table 4, PDF Page 13 (p. 131)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The setting (34 African countries surveyed in 2016-2018 under Afrobarometer Round 7 CAPI protocols across subnational regions such as States, Administrative Districts, and Provinces, and enumeration areas) and sample characteristics are adequately described via Table 1 summary statistics (access rate, bribery prevalence, piped infrastructure coverage, lived poverty index, urban share, and gender balance) and country-level examples (e.g., Guinea vs. Mauritius), with full country-by-country summary statistics provided in online Appendix Table A1.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 4 (Data and Methods), PDF Pages 7-9 (pp. 125-127); Table 1, PDF Page 7 (p. 125)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Although using direct bribery experience collected via CAPI avoids expert-perception circularity, the exposure measure has major construct validity and reliability limitations for water corruption: (1) the Afrobarometer item asks simultaneously about water, sanitation, and electric services rather than water specifically; (2) respondents who had no experience seeking services are coded zero alongside those who sought services without paying a bribe; (3) regional corruption averages subnational survey responses of varying sample sizes; and (4) applying the measure to Rounds 5 and 6 yields null and opposite-signed associations.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 4 (Data and Methods), PDF Page 8 (p. 126); Section 5 (Results/Discussion), PDF Page 12 (p. 130)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: No objective technical or physical criteria were used to measure either local water infrastructure conditions or household water supply status. Local piped infrastructure (pipes_i) relies on whether the survey enumerator believed there was a piped water system most houses could access, and household water deprivation relies entirely on respondent subjective judgment of having 'enough clean water'.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 4 (Data and Methods), PDF Pages 7 and 9 (pp. 125, 127)

domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly identify key household, infrastructural, and contextual confounders, including the household's own quid pro quo bribery, presence of local piped water infrastructure, household lived poverty, urban versus rural location, respondent gender, general non-utilities corruption in the region, and time-invariant country-level factors.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3, PDF Page 6 (p. 124); Section 4 (Data and Methods), PDF Pages 8-9 (pp. 126-127); Section 5, PDF Page 11 (p. 129)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors state and implement multiple strategies to address confounding: multivariable control for individual bribery, area piped infrastructure, lived poverty index, urban status, gender, and regional non-utilities corruption; country fixed effects; sample stratification by presence of piped water infrastructure; mixed-effects models; and explicit abstention from causal claims due to remaining cross-sectional endogeneity and unmeasured subnational confounders.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 4 (Data and Methods), PDF Pages 8-9 (pp. 126-127); Section 5 (Results/Discussion), PDF Pages 10-12 (pp. 128-130)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Outcomes are measured using standardized Afrobarometer CAPI household items (past-year frequency of going without enough clean water for home use, and whether the main water source is inside the house, compound, or outside). While ordered probit models address the coarse binary cutoff of the primary Access dummy (which groups 'many times' without water with 'never'), self-reported 12-month recall of 'clean water' lacks objective microbiological/chemical quality or service-continuity validation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 4 (Data and Methods), PDF Page 7 (p. 125); Section 5 (Results/Discussion), PDF Pages 11-13 (pp. 129-131); Endnote 6, PDF Page 14 (p. 132)

domain_ratings.justification: Binary probit and ordered probit models reporting marginal effects with country fixed effects and region-clustered standard errors are appropriate for binary and ordinal cross-sectional survey outcomes. The authors also verify robustness using mixed-effects models (random intercepts and slopes), PSU-level corruption measures, and a leave-one-out regional corruption measure excluding the respondent's own bribery report (Endnote 5).

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This analytical cross-sectional study analyzes Afrobarometer Round 7 household survey data (N = 44,778 across 34 African countries, 2016-2018) using binary and ordered probit models with country fixed effects and region-clustered standard errors to examine the association between regional utilities bribery and household access to clean water. Appraised with the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies, the study raises Some concern overall. Methodological strengths include large multi-country CAPI survey coverage, multivariable adjustment (individual bribery, area piped infrastructure, lived poverty, urbanicity, gender, regional non-utilities corruption, and country fixed effects), extensive specification checks (ordered probit, mixed-effects, leave-one-out regional incidence, and piped vs. non-piped stratification), and commendably transparent reporting—including an explicit disclaimer against causal claims and disclosure that earlier survey rounds (Rounds 5 and 6) show null or opposite-signed associations. Key sources of bias include exposure misclassification (the bribery question bundles water, sanitation, and electricity services together and codes non-seekers of services as zero), subjective self-reported outcome and enumerator infrastructure measures without objective water quality or continuity verification, potential reverse causality, and unmeasured subnational/regional confounders (e.g., regional economic capacity, climate, and utility governance).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Analytical cross-sectional observational household survey study (multi-country binary probit and ordered probit regression analysis using Afrobarometer Round 7 data)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design, survey description, variable operationalization, probit/ordered probit model specification, confounder controls, and causal disclaimers are in Section 4 (Data and Methods, PDF Pages 7-9 / pp. 125-127) and Section 1 (Introduction, PDF Page 2 / p. 120). Main regressions, subgroup splits by piped infrastructure, ordered probit checks, Round 5/6 comparisons, and water source location models are in Section 5 (Results/Discussion, PDF Pages 9-13 / pp. 127-131) and Endnotes 4-6 (PDF Page 14 / p. 132), referencing online Supporting Information Tables A1-A6.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study analyzes cross-sectional observational household survey data from Round 7 of the Afrobarometer (2016-2018) to estimate statistical associations between regional utilities bribery incidence and self-reported water access using probit and ordered probit regressions, without any discrete policy/intervention comparator or quasi-experimental identification strategy (and explicitly disclaims causal inference). Therefore, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching appraisal tool under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
